name: Either-Or Subset Sum (EOSS)
description: Either-Or Subset Sum (EOSS) is a hybrid total-search variant introduced by Tim Randolph (PhD thesis, Columbia 2024, Chapter 4, based on the 2023 preprint 'A Hybrid Algorithm for Subset Sum and Equal Subset Sum'). Given an instance X = {x_1,...,x_n}, t of Subset Sum, the algorithm must return EITHER a subset of X summing to t (a vanilla Subset Sum witness) OR two distinct subsets of X with equal sum (an Equal-Subset-Sum / ESS witness). Equivalently it asks for a solution to Generalized Subset Sum on either of the two smallest natural coefficient sets, C = {0,1} (Subset Sum) or C = {-1,0,1} (Equal Subset Sum). EOSS is presented as a concrete benchmark for the 'structure vs. randomness' programme and as explicit evidence towards the formal Meet-in-the-Middle conjecture, because it shows that a natural problem closely related to vanilla Subset Sum can be solved in worst-case time 2^{(0.5-eps)n} with eps > 0.03, i.e. below the long-standing 2^{n/2} barrier. It is not a promise problem: a 'No' answer is allowed when neither an SS nor an ESS solution exists, and the algorithm makes no false-positive claims.
worst_case_time: O*(2^{0.461n}) randomized worst-case (Theorem 6 of Randolph's thesis), i.e. O(2^{(0.5-eps)n}) with eps = 0.039 > 0.03. This beats both the meet-in-the-middle barrier O*(2^{0.5n}) and the then-best worst-case Equal-Subset-Sum algorithm O*(3^{0.488n}) = O*(1.7088^n) of Mucha-Nederlof-Pawlewicz-Wegrzycki (ESA 2019). The thesis also reports, in a remark, that a careful modification of Algorithm 1 of Austrin-Kaski-Koivisto-Nederlof (2016) yields a full EOSS solution in O*(2^{0.421n}) (and that the decision variant is implicit in that work at O*(2^{0.480n})).
space_complexity: Not specified as a headline bound; the algorithm builds MITM-style candidate lists and a mod-p dynamic-programming table, so its space is comparable to its time for the list-based phases (the thesis analyses runtime, not space, and no space-optimized EOSS algorithm is stated).
model: Standard word RAM / unit-cost RAM with O(log(sum of inputs))-bit words; the EOSS result is a classical (non-quantum) exponential-time algorithm.
randomized_or_deterministic: Monte Carlo with one-sided error: never returns a false positive and succeeds with probability 1 - o(1) on every input (internal randomness: a random prime p, random residue r, and random subsampling; success can be amplified by repetition).
time_space_tradeoff_curve: single point (no time-space tradeoff family is presented for EOSS).
numerical_exponent_and_record_year: Base 2, exponent 0.461 (equivalently 0.5 - eps with eps = 0.039), from Randolph's 2024 thesis / 2023 preprint; an alternative claimed bound of 2^{0.421n} is noted. Record year: 2023/2024.
problem_variant: Either-Or / hybrid Subset Sum: solve either vanilla Subset Sum (C = {0,1}) or Equal Subset Sum (C = {-1,0,1}, target 0) on the same input. Closely related to 'Sum-Pigeon' and to the total-search class PPP (Papadimitriou 1994), though unlike Pigeon a negative answer is allowed.
applies_to: Given n integers X and target t, return either A with sum(A) = t or two distinct A, B with sum(A) = sum(B). No density restriction and no promise on the input; the guarantee is only that a witness for whichever sub-problem admits one is returned with high probability.
coefficient_set: C = {0,1} for the Subset Sum branch (|C| = 2) and C = {-1,0,1} for the Equal Subset Sum branch (|C| = 3); EOSS is the task of solving Generalized Subset Sum on either coefficient set.
density_regime: Density-agnostic: EOSS is a worst-case statement over all inputs, with no assumption on d = n/log2(max|a_i|).
solution_regime: Hybrid / no promise. Unlike Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum, existence is not guaranteed; the algorithm may answer 'No' when neither an SS nor an ESS solution exists.
cardinality_constraint: No fixed-cardinality or Hamming-layer constraint is imposed.
key_technique: Structure-vs-randomness dichotomy combined with an adaptation of the Howgrave-Graham-Joux Representation Method to worst-case (not average-case) inputs: (i) modified meet-in-the-middle if a small Subset Sum solution exists; (ii) modified meet-in-the-middle if a small ESS solution exists; (iii) a structural lemma proving that an SS instance whose solution has few distinct subset sums is an easy ESS instance; (iv) otherwise, hashing partial candidate solutions into residue classes modulo a large random prime so that many distinct small subset sums 'mix' and many residue pairs (r, t-r) contain a solution pair; (v) a recovery step that either finds a pair or, if it sees too many colliding partial candidates, returns those collisions as an ESS solution.
core_idea: Partition instances into random-like and structured. Random-like/large-signature instances let the representation method's partial candidates hash evenly modulo a random prime, so a matching pair is found by MITM and pairwise candidate checks; structured instances, where a Subset Sum solution admits only few distinct subset sums, are shown to automatically yield a small Equal Subset Sum solution that MITM recovers. In the only remaining case the collisions encountered during recovery themselves constitute an ESS witness. The hybrid output ('either-or') is what allows the algorithm to keep the worst-case guarantee below 2^{n/2}.
reduction_pipeline: No reduction to an external problem. Internally it combines (a) a two-half meet-in-the-middle over the n inputs, (b) bucketing partial candidate solutions by their value modulo a random prime p (random restriction to a residue class), and (c) the representation method's signature/collision machinery. Conceptually EOSS is a 'sum-flavored' specialization of the Pigeon problem / PPP circuitry C(X): {0,1}^n -> {0,1}^n.
constructive_vs_existential: Constructive: on success it returns an explicit witness (a subset summing to t, or a colliding pair of subsets).
search_vs_decision_witness: Returns an explicit witness for either sub-problem; it never outputs a false positive and may output 'No'. Constructivity is proved for the randomized algorithm (probability 1 - o(1)).
obstacle_to_2n3: EOSS reaches exponent 0.461 (eps = 0.039) but does not solve vanilla Subset Sum (C = {0,1}); the 'either-or' escape to an ESS witness is essential. Structural results of the thesis indicate that instances defeating the current MITM/representation approaches are exactly those admitting small ESS solutions, so a 2^{(0.5-eps)n} bound for vanilla Subset Sum would require exploiting structure in the remaining hard regime without an ESS fallback. The exponent is small (0.039) and not shown optimal, and no time-space tradeoff is derived.
potential_to_break_mitm: Medium for the programme, low-to-medium for vanilla Subset Sum. EOSS is direct evidence that a natural sibling of Subset Sum can be solved below 2^{n/2} unconditionally, sharpening the circumstantial case for the (positive) formal MITM conjecture; but the two hard cases remain C = {-1,1} (Partition / Subset Sum) and C = {-2,-1,1,2}, where MITM has still not been beaten in the worst case (Randolph-Wegrzycki, STOC 2026).
barrier_evidence: There is no unconditional 2^{Omega(n)} lower bound for Subset Sum and ETH only rules out 2^{o(n)}; SETH gives pseudo-polynomial conditional lower bounds (Abboud-Bringmann-Hermelin-Shabtay) that do not forbid 2^{(1/2-eps)n}. Consequently the formal Meet-in-the-Middle conjecture (Randolph's thesis, Conjecture 1: there exists eps > 0 such that vanilla Subset Sum can be solved in time O(2^{(0.5-eps)n})) is an open positive conjecture, not a barrier. EOSS itself is a barrier-softening result: it shows a close variant breaks 2^{n/2} in the worst case, while the 3SUM/4SUM and k-SUM conjectures constrain only the structured-matching steps a general 2^{n/3} algorithm would need.
open_questions: Can the structure-vs-randomness approach be extended from EOSS to vanilla Subset Sum (or Partition), i.e. remove the ESS escape hatch? What is the best achievable exponent for EOSS (0.461, or the reported 0.421 via AKKN16 techniques, or lower)? Can EOSS be derandomized? Is there a matching conditional lower bound pinning the EOSS exponent? Can EOSS techniques combine with the worst-case representation/mixing machinery (Randolph-Wegrzycki) or log-shaving (Chen-Jin-Randolph-Servedio) to push vanilla Subset Sum?
conditional_hypothesis: No assumption is needed for the EOSS upper bound (unconditional, randomized, one-sided error). The result is offered as evidence for the positive formal Meet-in-the-Middle conjecture of Randolph's thesis (Conjecture 1), which is itself unproven. Lower bounds for related problems rest on ETH, SETH (pseudo-polynomial regime) and PPP-completeness conjectures (Papadimitriou 1994).
worst_case_vs_average_case_guarantee: Worst-case guarantee: for every n-integer instance the randomized algorithm succeeds with probability 1 - o(1) (amplifiable) and never returns a false positive. Randomness is internal to the algorithm, not assumed on the input.
cryptographic_regime: Indirect. EOSS uses and adapts the representation technique that underlies hard-knapsack cryptanalysis (Howgrave-Graham-Joux, Becker-Coron-Joux), and its dichotomy is relevant to density ~1 knapsacks, but it is an exact worst-case algorithmic result rather than an attack; no specific density/sample-key parameters are given.
pseudopolynomial_interaction: None in the stated result (EOSS ignores the numeric magnitude of items). The related number-balancing / Karmarkar-Karp differencing ideas appear in the same thesis but are not combined with EOSS.

empirical_evidence: None reported: the result is a combinatorial/probabilistic analysis with a proof (randomized one-sided-error algorithm); no benchmark experiments.
implementation_artifact: none found (no reference code or repository published).
verification_method: Reproduce the proof of Theorem 6: (1) check the structural Lemma 18 ('ESS instances with small solutions are easy') and the signature-distribution/solution-size bounds; (2) verify the mod-p residue-class mixing argument (many distinct small subset sums distribute over residue pairs); (3) confirm the recovery step returns an SS pair or a genuine ESS collision; (4) run the two MITM branches and the representation branch on random and on near-geometric structured instances and confirm success probability 1 - o(1) and the O*(2^{0.461n}) complexity; compare against brute force and MITM on small n.
